edits.name: A watch on one public page or feed Tony names
edits.description: Tony names one public page or feed, and a small script with no model checks it during the day and texts him once when something new appears there; otherwise it stays silent. If the source is a team or school schedule with a subscription link, it is first subscribed into the shared Google calendar, which needs no code. Storm alerts and recall notices are not watched: weather answers already carry active alerts for home, and the phones and the agencies send their own.
edits.example: Trigger: the feed Tony registered shows an item the script has not seen before. Text: 'Page watch: new on the page you asked me to watch: <the item's title> <its link on that site>'. On a day with nothing new, no text is sent.
edits.how: Tony names the page or feed at execution. Step 1, no code: if it is a schedule with a subscription link, a parent subscribes it into the shared Google calendar, where calendar answers (F009) read it. Step 2, only if that is not enough: one reviewed script, run as one host command job (`--command-argv`, no model call) created by the jobs script (G003), with the owner's handle read from the family file, a time limit and daytime hours Tony sets. The script uses the site's feed when there is one, otherwise a plain https GET and a text hash; it checks the address itself (https, public host), keeps seen ids in a state file, and prints one templated line that starts with its label, or `NO_REPLY`. Tony's job first; Jordan's copy is a second job with its own state file. Not built: storm, recall and keyword-list scripts. No rule in the house-rules plugin.
depends_on: Tony provides the one page or feed to watch at execution (and its subscription link, if it is a schedule)
Tony provides the daytime hours for the check at execution
G003 in its small form: the three scheduler switches and the short jobs script, which creates the watch as one command job
F009 calendar read, only for the no-code route (a schedule subscribed into the shared Google calendar then shows in calendar answers)
caveats: A parent cannot start a watch from chat: command jobs are created by the operator, so the watch, and any second page later, is a request to Tony.
The watch gives no earlier notice than the source's own service: a team app's push is faster for a same-day change.

A hash watch on a page can fire on changes that do not matter; pages that need JavaScript or a login are out of reach, and many school portals publish no feed. The watch never runs on a logged-in page.

Command jobs run on the Gateway host as the happy user, outside the sandbox, agent tool policy and OpenClaw's fetch guardrails, so the script checks its address itself (https, public host) and is reviewed like the rest of the config repo.
A team's subscription link is a bearer secret, so it sits in a file only the happy user can read and stays out of family.json5 if that file is committed.

Not built: storm, recall and keyword-list scripts. Silence from the watch is never an all-clear, since Happy is down in a power cut or a network outage; the phones' own emergency and severe-weather alerts stay on, and recall emails from the agencies' own sign-ups arrive in the 07:00 mail text.
edits.safety: No model reads the page: the script prints a fixed line with the outside title stripped and capped, and only a link on the registered site. It fetches only the address Tony registered and sends nothing about the family out. The text goes to the job's owner alone, from the handle in the family file. No agent gains a tool.
unverified: Whether the page Tony names publishes a feed, or can be read at all without JavaScript or a login; checked first at execution.
Whether a schedule subscribed into Google Calendar is visible to Happy's read-only calendar tool (F009), so that the no-code route is enough.

That the jobs script can create a command job from the deploy path (T3), and how the outbound firewall, once it blocks by default, treats a fetch made by a command job's script.

edits.name: Sick-day log of what was given, shared by both parents
edits.description: When a child is ill, both parents text Happy what they gave and when, and either can ask 'when was the last dose?' and get the same answer: the last dose that was logged, who logged it and how long ago. Happy records and recalls; it never advises a dose, and every answer ends with a line to check the label. The log puts the children's dose notes on the cloud model, which Tony confirms at execution.
edits.example: Jordan texts: 'The kindergartner has a fever, gave the children's acetaminophen at 7:40.' Happy confirms: 'Logged: children's acetaminophen at 7:40 this morning.' Later Tony texts: 'When was the last dose?' and gets: 'Last dose logged: children's acetaminophen at 7:40 this morning, logged by Jordan, 3 hours 5 minutes ago. Check the label for dose and timing, and ask the pediatrician or poison control if unsure.'
edits.how: One dose table in the household database (F031), with two tools on both parents' own agents. Logging stores which child (a short label), what was given as typed, the time and which parent's agent logged it. The time is the Mac's clock when the tool runs unless the parent states one; a stated time ('at 7:40') is read by the model, so Happy's confirmation spells it out in full, day included. `care_last` returns the latest rows, the elapsed minutes (subtracted in code) and one fixed line: check the label, ask the pediatrician or poison control if unsure. The agent answers normally under one AGENTS.md rule, never advise a dose, with one eval case. Each tool run deletes rows older than 14 days. Not built: a canned reply, a timed sweep, an ask relayed to the other parent, any rule in the house-rules plugin. Absence-note drafts, tomorrow's calendar and a check-in reminder (Tony only) are ordinary requests.

Happy knows only the doses that were texted to it. A dose given and not logged is missing from the answer, so the reply says 'last dose logged' and who logged it, never 'last dose given'.

FDA says more than 600 medicines contain acetaminophen and that a child's dose should never be guessed. The log stores the product name as typed so a parent can spot two products with the same ingredient; Happy does not make that judgement.

A poison centre's advice is that the log should stay with the medicine and be marked at every dose. Happy's log is not next to the bottle and cannot be reached when Happy, the network or the cloud model is down, so it works beside a note kept with the medicine and does not replace one.

The 14-day deletion covers the log rows only; the chat transcript still holds what was typed and follows the general retention setting. 'Never advise a dose' is an instruction backed by a test case, not a hard limit.
